clue.text: Idle talk by English conductor behind piano

indicators.note: behind places the conductor's name after the piano letter in the across-reading order of the answer

parts.note: p is the musical abbreviation for piano, meaning softly
Sir Simon Rattle is a famous English orchestral conductor

explanation.surface: Someone grumbles about an English conductor chattering away behind the piano.
explanation.walkthrough: 'behind' puts the conductor after P; 'by' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Prattle is chatter of a silly, trivial kind, which is exactly idle talk.

clue.text: Rather pale shout, nothing long

parts.note: to shout is to yell
O looks like zero, so it stands for nothing
to long for something is to wish for it

explanation.surface: A pale person shouts and gets nothing back, longing in vain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'long' looks like an adjective but works as the verb meaning yearn.
explanation.definitionFit: The suffix -ish means somewhat, so a yellowish face is somewhat pale, tinged with a sickly colour.

clue.text: Treble in medley is one who sings forcefully

indicators.note: a medley is a jumble or mixture, so the letters of the word treble are mixed up

explanation.surface: A boy treble in a medley of songs turns out to be a loud singer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in medley' tells you to rearrange the letters of TREBLE; 'is' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A belter is a singer with a powerful voice who belts out songs at full volume.

clue.text: Stop drink with journalists

parts.note: to sup is to drink, in small mouthfuls
the press is the collective name for journalists

explanation.surface: An instruction to quit drinking with the reporters.
explanation.definitionFit: To suppress something is to put a stop to it, as a government might stop a protest.

clue.text: Number two is nothing here

definitions.meaning: a deputy, the person ranked just below the leader
nothing is the letter O, and the letter O is the second letter of the word command, so the answer describes where it stands

explanation.surface: A deputy complains that they count for nothing in this place.
explanation.walkthrough: The second reading is cryptic: 'nothing' is O, and O sits in second place in COMMAND. 'is' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A deputy is the person next in rank below the leader, ready to take over when needed.

clue.text: Medium taken up in fright from extensive disease

indicators.note: in signals that the reversed piece sits inside the word for fright

parts.note: panic is sudden fright

indicators.note: in a down clue taken up means the word is read from bottom to top, so it runs backwards

parts.note: MED is a standard abbreviation for medium, as on clothing size labels

explanation.surface: A spiritualist medium, swept up in alarm, flees a widespread illness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Medium' looks like a psychic but is the size abbreviation; 'taken up', in a down clue, turns MED into DEM, and 'in' puts it inside PANIC.
explanation.definitionFit: A pandemic is an epidemic that spreads across a whole country or the world, a disease over a very wide area.

clue.text: Jumper's on back to front? Have a rest!

indicators.note: on means placed next to, so the last letter follows the kangaroo piece

parts.note: a roo, short for kangaroo, is a jumper, and the apostrophe s adds an S

indicators.note: back to is read as the back of, so only the final letter of the word front is used

explanation.surface: Someone has put their sweater on back to front and is told to sit down and relax.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jumper' suggests a sweater worn back to front, but it is a kangaroo. 'back to front' gives T, the back letter of FRONT.
explanation.definitionFit: To roost is to settle down for rest or sleep, as birds do on a perch at night.

clue.text: Drink bargains (but not British) all over the shop

indicators.note: all over the shop is slang for in total disarray, so the remaining letters of the word bargains are scrambled

explanation.surface: Cheap offers on a drink, though not British ones, are everywhere in the store.
explanation.walkthrough: 'but not' takes the B of British out of BARGAINS, and 'all over the shop' rearranges the letters left.
explanation.definitionFit: Sangria is a Spanish punch of red wine, fruit and soda, a drink served chilled.

clue.text: Type of block that's an easy thing to make ?

definitions.meaning: a building block made from cinders bound with cement, called by this name in Britain
informally something done with no effort at all, a doddle

explanation.surface: A builder muses on which kind of block is easiest to make.
explanation.walkthrough: A breeze block is a British building block of cinders and cement; 'a breeze' is also slang for something easy. 'that's' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A breeze block is a lightweight cinder building block, and a breeze is informal for a task done with no trouble.

clue.text: Hundred discovered outside on floor

indicators.note: outside means the two letter groups for hundred and discovered sit around the word on

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred
something discovered has been found
taken as written

explanation.surface: A hundred of something is found lying out on the floor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'floor' looks like the ground underfoot but is the verb meaning baffle; 'outside' wraps the hundred and discovered pieces around the little word on.
explanation.definitionFit: To floor someone is to baffle or bewilder them completely, leaving them utterly perplexed.

clue.text: This tilts toe when badly fitted?

definitions.text: This tilts toe when badly fitted?

indicators.note: something badly fitted has its parts put together in the wrong order, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A complaint about a high-heeled shoe that tips the foot forward when it fits badly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'badly fitted' rearranges TILTS TOE, and the whole clue also describes a very high heel pitching the toes forward.
explanation.definitionFit: A stiletto is a woman's shoe with a very high, thin heel that pitches the foot forward onto the toes.

clue.text: Squeeze former partner, tense by the sound of it

parts.note: an ex is a former spouse or partner

indicators.note: by the sound of it means the word for tense is said aloud and spelt as a different word

parts.note: tense means stretched tight, taut

explanation.surface: Someone tries to squeeze their ex, who sounds tense about it.
explanation.walkthrough: In a non-rhotic British accent TAUT and TORT sound the same.
explanation.definitionFit: To squeeze someone is to force money or favours out of them by pressure, as a blackmailer does.

clue.text: Fellow let down opened out

parts.note: F is an abbreviation for fellow, as in FRS, Fellow of the Royal Society
to let something down is to lower it

explanation.surface: A man feels let down by someone who then opened up to him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'let down' suggests disappointment but means physically lowered.
explanation.definitionFit: A bud that has flowered has opened out into bloom.

clue.text: I'm keeping quiet in Islamic republic, being one from western Europe

indicators.note: in places the combined piece inside the name of the Islamic republic

parts.note: Iran is officially the Islamic Republic of Iran

indicators.note: keeping means holding something inside, so the quiet letters go within the letters of I'm

parts.note: taken as written, without the apostrophe
sh is the sound used to ask for quiet

explanation.surface: Someone keeps a low profile in Iran, being a native of western Europe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'keeping' and 'in' nest the pieces one inside another; Iran is officially called the Islamic Republic of Iran.
explanation.definitionFit: A native of Ireland, an island nation on the western edge of Europe.

clue.text: Such is thesis becoming this insensitive

definitions.meaning: the word thesis loses its middle two letters and becomes the word this, so it is literally without its centre
unfeeling, cold and uncaring towards others

explanation.surface: A critic calls a student's thesis cold and unfeeling.
explanation.walkthrough: Take the middle, or heart, out of THESIS and it becomes THIS; the answer describes that change.
explanation.definitionFit: A cruel, unfeeling person is said to have no heart, so insensitive behaviour is called that.

clue.text: Greek has three articles about northern Ireland

indicators.note: about means going around, so the three articles surround the abbreviation

parts.note: a, the and an are the three articles of English grammar
a, the and an are the three articles of English grammar
a, the and an are the three articles of English grammar

explanation.surface: A Greek man carries three newspaper articles about Northern Ireland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts the three English articles (A, THE, AN) around NI, the usual abbreviation for Northern Ireland.
explanation.definitionFit: A citizen of Athens, the Greek capital, is a Greek.

clue.text: Wretched route, and the rest restricts one

parts.note: a path is a route

indicators.note: restricts means holds within limits, so the letters for and the rest enclose the letter for one

parts.note: etc, short for et cetera, means and the rest
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A miserable route, and everything else on it holds someone back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'restricts' puts I inside ETC to make ETIC; 'and' before 'the rest' belongs to that phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Pathetic means pitiful or miserable, deserving sorrow or contempt.

clue.text: Make good journey in single attempt

parts.note: to atone is to make amends, to make good a wrong
to go is to journey or travel

explanation.surface: Advice to make a good journey by doing it in one try.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Make good' looks like praise for the journey but means make amends.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something all in one try, without pausing or repeating, is doing it in a single attempt.

clue.text: Rock I'd say, in case of "garage" is not middle of the road

indicators.note: in places the jumbled letters inside the outer pair
the case of a word is its outer shell, so only the first and last letters of the quoted word are kept

parts.note: the setter's slip: he meant the name of the singer Amy Winehouse, and confused one storage building for another

indicators.note: to rock is to shake about, so the letters of I'd say are jumbled

explanation.surface: A rock fan, speaking of garage music, says it is not mainstream.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter has admitted a slip: he meant 'Winehouse' (the singer Amy Winehouse), whose first and last letters W and E surround AYSID, the anagram of I'D SAY made by 'Rock'. As printed, 'garage' gives G and E.
explanation.definitionFit: The wayside is the edge or verge beside a road, so it is the opposite of the centre of the carriageway.

clue.text: Rash aggressive youth losing his head on crack

indicators.note: on in an across clue means placed after, so the crack word follows
losing his head means the youth's word drops its first letter

parts.note: a lout is a rough, aggressive young man
a crack is a break

explanation.surface: An aggressive young man loses his temper over drugs and comes out in spots.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rash' reads as an adjective describing the youth, but it is the noun. 'losing his head' leaves OUT, and 'on' sets the crack word after it.
explanation.definitionFit: A rash is a sudden outbreak of spots on the skin, and the word also means any sudden spread.

clue.text: Harangue one in business

indicators.note: in places the letter for one inside the word for business

parts.note: trade is commerce or business
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Someone launches into a rant about a single person in the company.
explanation.definitionFit: A tirade is a long, angry speech of criticism, the same as a harangue.

clue.text: Search in favour of distinct historical period

parts.note: for means supporting, in favour of
an age is a distinct period of history, such as the Bronze Age

explanation.surface: A historian searches for evidence of a particular era.
explanation.definitionFit: To forage is to search about for food or supplies.

clue.text: Explosive crowd in airline showing up

indicators.note: in a down clue showing up means the combined letters are read from the bottom upwards
in places the crowd word inside the airline initials

parts.note: BA is British Airways
a mob is an unruly crowd

explanation.surface: A crowd turns up at the airline offices, causing an explosive scene.
explanation.walkthrough: 'showing up', in a down clue, reads the crowd-inside-airline letters (BMOBA) from the bottom upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: An atomic bomb is a nuclear explosive device.

clue.text: Puritan rather backing off before adult catalogue

indicators.note: before places the shortened word ahead of the remaining pieces
backing off means the back letter of the word is taken off

parts.note: more can mean rather, as in more dead than alive
A is the film-rating abbreviation for adult
a list is a catalogue

explanation.surface: A prude backs away rather than face an adult catalogue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backing off' drops the last letter of MORE, leaving MOR.
explanation.definitionFit: A strait-laced person who lectures others on right and wrong is a puritan.

clue.text: What could be for pudding? Answer is a lemon confection

indicators.note: a confection is something put together or concocted, so the letters of is a lemon are mixed up

explanation.surface: Someone asks what's for dessert and is told it is a lemon sweet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Answer' is only a link here: the fodder is IS A LEMON, and 'confection' rearranges it.
explanation.definitionFit: Semolina is a coarse wheat meal boiled with milk and sugar to make a classic British school dessert.

clue.text: What's said at wedding by parties dancing

indicators.note: by means next to, so the vow is placed beside the parties word

parts.note: dos are parties, as in a leaving do
I do is the vow spoken by bride and groom

explanation.surface: A guest notes the vows spoken at a wedding by both people taking part, before the dancing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'parties' looks like the bride and groom but means social do's.
explanation.definitionFit: A do-si-do is a square-dance figure in which partners circle back to back, a move made while dancing.

clue.text: Income bond on going bust merged

indicators.note: bust means broken, so the remaining letters of income bond are scrambled

explanation.surface: An investor's income bond has gone bust and been absorbed into another.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on going' removes ON from INCOME BOND, and 'bust' rearranges what is left.
explanation.definitionFit: Things combined have been joined together into one, which is what merged means.
